results.title: Nscale Posts $1.02B Net Loss in H1, Nebius GPU Rental Rates Rise Up to 21% | BroadChain.info
highlights:

OpenAI's internal forecasts show cumulative free cash flow from 2026 to 2030 will be negative $278 billion, mainly due to continued massive investment in model training, inference, and infrastructure. The company expects revenue of approximately $36 billion in 2026, growing to $350 billion by 2030, with cumulative spending on computing power and related infrastructure over five years reaching approximately $856 billion, with expenditure scale continuing to exceed operating cash flow.

...

AI cloud service provider Nebius announced that starting October 1, it will raise on-demand rental prices for some Nvidia GPUs, the second price increase within three months. The price per GPU hour for H100 rose from $3.85 to $4.50, an increase of about 17%; H200 rose from $4.50 to $5.40, an increase of 20%; B200 and B300 rose to $8.50 and $9.50 respectively. Nebius once again raised on-demand quotes, OpenAI expects free cash flow outflow of $278 billion over the next five years, and Oracle-related data center loans are seeing discounts and distribution difficulties. There are still pricing signals on the demand side, but whether projects can obtain funding, be delivered on schedule, and generate revenue will affect subsequent expansion.

results.title: GPU price index 2026: cloud rental surge versus retail volatility | SpecForge
highlights:
1. Cloud GPU rental prices for the newest cohort rose from $2.12/hr in October 2024 to $4.72/hr by September 2026, while Legacy silicon fell from $1.77 to $0.95 over the same window, per the AIMultiple index covering 17 models across 75 providers [S4].
2. Retail-side GPU tracking is dominated by Tom's Hardware's daily price index and Semianalysis's cloud-rental composite [S1][S2].

...

The newest-generation cloud GPU cohort (B200, B300, MI300X, RTX 5090) saw on-demand median hourly rental rise from $2.12 in October 2024 to $4.72 in September 2026, while the Modern cohort (H100, H200, A100, L40S, RTX 4090, A10G, T4, L4) moved from $1.35 to $1.45 over the same period [S4].

The Legacy silicon cohort (V100, P100, K80, M60, P40) saw its on-demand median hourly rental fall from $1.77 in October 2024 to $0.95 in September 2026 [S4]. The divergence is the dominant signal in the 2026 GPU pricing landscape.

...

The AIMultiple index groups 17 tracked SKUs into three fixed cohorts to keep the time series comparable even as individual listings churn [S4]. Each GPU contributes equally to its group median, so a single provider's price cut does not skew the cohort. The Last released cohort (2024 and later) has the steepest curve: B200 and B300 medians now sit at $6.52 and $7.87 per GPU-hour on-demand, while MI300X runs at $2.91, undercutting H100 at $3.25 [S4]. RTX 5090 at $0.63 and RTX 4090 at $0.44 reflect consumer-card economics entering the rental pool, with the 4090 still widely available at 68% of tracked listings and the 5090 at 79% [S4].

MI300X reserved pricing reverses the usual discount pattern: its reserved median of $3.39 sits above the $2.91 on-demand median, a signal that long-term MI300X commitments are scarce enough to carry a premium, while B300's reserved median of $5.71 against its $7.87 on-demand still delivers a conventional 27% discount for committed terms [S4]. H100's reserved and on-demand gap is only $0.13 ($3.10 versus $3.23), reflecting mature supply [S4].

...

Provider choice adds a second axis of price variation. September 2026 H200 on-demand listings span $2.09 per GPU-hour at Beam to $13.78 at Microsoft Azure, a 6.6x spread that reflects differences in instance configuration, stock state, and data-residency tier rather than raw hardware markup [S4]. IONOS prices H100 and H200 as flat $3,990 monthly dedicated servers with EU data residency, a billing model that hides the hourly rate but is competitive against the $3.25 to $4.40 hourly H100/H200 medians for buyers needing residency guarantees [S4].

...

## Supply availability signals and MI300X scarcity

Confirmed availability as a share of all tracked listings is lowest for MI300X at 7%, followed by B300 at 11% and B200 at 16% [S4]. H100 confirms availability on 33% of listings, while RTX 4090 and RTX 5090 reach 68% and 79% respectively, the consumer-card ceiling where almost every listed instance is actively rentable [S4]. However, 88% of MI300X listings carry unknown stock status, so the 7% confirmed-available figure cannot be inverted to mean 93% sold out, the denominator includes available, unknown, waitlisted, and unavailable entries across all billing tiers [S4].

For a procurement team reading the index, the actionable signal is provider-count and listing-count, not the confirmed-available percentage in isolation. A 7% confirmed rate across 40 listings is stronger evidence of scarcity than a 7% rate across 5 listings, and the index does not currently publish the listing-count denominator publicly [S4].

...

Hourly rental rate alone does not measure workload cost. The 2026 GPU index recommends pairing the rental table with a multi-GPU benchmark covering H100, H200, B200, and MI300X to compute time-to-completion on representative training and inference workloads [S4]. A 1.8x faster GPU at 1.5x the hourly rate is cheaper per job, a calculation that flipped H200's value proposition in 2025 once NVLink and FP8 throughput differences were measured on production transformer training rather than peak FLOPS [S4].

On the consumer side, Pagecrawl's tracker identified two purchase-timing windows within any GPU generation: 6-9 months post-launch when supply stabilizes and board-partner competition widens, and the pre/post-next-gen transition when retailers discount remaining inventory to clear shelf space [S5]. The 2025 RTX 5080 example, a $999 MSRP card that held $1,149 or higher street pricing, saw a transient drop to $1,029 at Best Buy as the only sub-$1,149 print captured in the public example [S5].

...

For a hyperscale or neocloud capacity buyer, the dominant 2026 signal is the 122% rise in newest-cohort on-demand pricing against flat Modern pricing, which means the cost of stepping up to B200/B300 has roughly doubled since late 2024 while the cost of staying on H100/A100 has not [S4]. The H200 6.6x provider spread ($2.09 to $13.78) is the next-most-actionable number, because a workload that runs acceptably on H200 can be cost-cut by 5-6x simply by changing provider, with residency and managed-service features as the trade-off [S4].

For a consumer or workstation buyer, the actionable signals are the 68-79% availability on RTX 4090/5090 listings (deep rental supply, weak secondary-market demand), the 7-16% availability on MI300X/B200/B300 (tight cloud supply, indicating vendor pull-through demand), and the two retail-timing windows at 6-9 months post-launch and at the generation transition [S4][S5]. Pairing the Tom's Hardware retail index with automated drop-alert tooling, as the Pagecrawl guide recommends, catches the 24-48 hour $100-300 dip windows that manual checking misses [S1][S5].

results.title: SpaceX Isn't CoreWeave's Real Problem | AInvest
highlights:
- Both companies compete for scarce 2026 GPU availability, with H100 lead times exceeding 50 weeks and memory shortages persisting until 2027.

- CoreWeave's $72B debt and 7:1 leverage ratio contrast with SpaceX's $60.7B net cash, exposing its vulnerability to GPU price declines post-2027.

- The real risk to CoreWeave CRWV-- is temporary GPU scarcity, not SpaceX SPCX-- - its $104B revenue backlog depends on a bottleneck that will normalize as Blackwell/Rubin architectures replace

...

The Anthropic deal works out to roughly $6 per GPU-hour for an H100 equivalent. That's not a price earthquake. It's roughly where CoreWeave already charges — CoreWeave lists an 8-GPU H100 instance at $49.24 per hour, which is $6.16 per GPU, with on-demand rates starting around $4.76 before you add CPU, memory, and storage. At $6 per GPU-hour, neither company is underpricing the other.

The claim that SpaceX is a new CoreWeave rival confuses a symptom for a diagnosis.

Both companies are competing for the same scarce resource in 2026: available GPU capacity that can be deployed right now, not on paper. The H100 faces lead times of 36 to 52 weeks through resellers. High-bandwidth memory, the actual binding constraint, is structurally undersupplied. TSMC's CoWoS packaging lines are fully allocated through at least mid-2027. NVIDIA itself reports what amounts to a $1 trillion GPU order backlog stretching through 2027.

In this environment, the company that already has 220,000 GPUs physically installed in a data center with 300 megawatts of dedicated power can charge premium rates. CoreWeave benefits from the exact same scarcity — its revenue backlog reached $104 billion as of June, up 246 percent year over year. The difference is that SpaceX's capacity was built to train its own Grok model; CoreWeave's capacity was always built to rent.

...

The broader market confirms the scarcity is real but narrowing. GPU contract pricing climbed roughly 40 percent between October 2025 and March 2026, driven by memory cost pass-throughs from Samsung and SK Hynix. But analyst expectations are for the CoWoS supply-demand gap to narrow from roughly 20 percent to 10 percent by year-end. The most likely relief comes in 2027, when frontier AI labs begin migrating their H100 inventory to Blackwell and Rubin architectures, returning older GPUs to the rental market.

When that happens, compute prices fall. They have always fallen — the used H100 market has already collapsed 85 percent from its 2023 peak, and marketplace providers today offer H100 capacity for as little as $1.38 per GPU-hour. The question isn't whether prices eventually drop; it's how fast they drop and which company survives the drop.

results.title: SpaceX's AI-Compute Leases Are Real. Its Delivered Capacity Isn't — Yet | AInvest
highlights:
- Google GOOGL-- agreed to pay SpaceX SPCX-- $920M/month for 110,000 NVIDIA NVDA-- GPUs (2026-2029), with termination rights if delivery fails by September 30, 2026.

- Additional leases with Anthropic ($1.25B/month) and Reflection AI ($150M/month) suggest $26B/year in AI compute commitments, but operational status remains unconfirmed.

- SpaceX's Tennessee facilities face cooling/power issues, with uptime below 99.9% and no verified active GPU blocks as of September 2026.

- AI compute pricing depends on deployed capacity, not announced contracts; CoreWeave's margins (59% EBITDA) remain stable despite speculative concerns.

- The key outcome hinges on September 30 delivery confirmation—actual GPU availability will determine market impact, not current lease agreements.

Google agreed to pay SpaceX SPCX-- $920 million a month for access to roughly 110,000 NVIDIA GPUs under a deal running from October 2026 through June 2029. If SpaceX fails to deliver the committed capacity by the September 30, 2026 deadline, Google GOOGL-- can terminate after a one-month grace period or accept fewer GPUs at a reduced fee. That contract is dated and confirmed. The conclusion people are building on top of it is not.

Here is the thesis making the rounds: a rocket-and-satellite outfit is piling GPUs into data centers, and the capacity influx will reprice AI compute and squeeze CoreWeave's margins. Treat the signed leases as live, operating supply and you have a real threat; treat them as paper and you mostly have a headline. The distinction decides whether this changes an investment view on CoreWeave CRWV-- at all.

...

The committed scale is not trivial. Anthropic took all of the Colossus 1 facility in Memphis, Tennessee for about $1.25 billion a month, and the Google deal alone runs $920 million a month for 32 months. A third arrangement signed in July gives Reflection AI access to NVIDIA NVDA-- GB300 chips at Colossus 2 for about $150 million a month. Take the two biggest and the annualized run-rate at stated monthly prices comes to roughly $26 billion a year.

## The delivery is not confirmed

Here is where the premise stops being engineering and starts being marketing. As of mid-September 2026 no dated record confirms a single committed external block is operating. The freshest reporting, dated September 3 — weeks before the Google deadline — says SpaceX replaced several of its AI-data-center leaders after its Tennessee and Mississippi facilities ran for months without backup cooling or power, kept alive by mobile gas turbines, Tesla Megapacks and more than 100 portable chillers, with uptime stuck below its own 99.9% target. Whether the ~110,000-GPU delivery to Google is met, delayed or renegotiated was still listed as an open item. Not confirmed online. Not delivered-and-energized.

 

The distinction carries the whole argument. AI-compute pricing is set by deployed, operating, energized supply against demand, not by announced contracts. A committed cluster is paper; it prices nothing until it is built, powered and running. So the honest state of the "influx" is a deadline that had not passed at this writing. Unconfirmed delivery is not the same as confirmed pricing pressure.

## The pricing and the margin record

Check the pricing record across the window these leases cover. SemiAnalysis reported H100 one-year rentals up about 40%, from $1.70 to $2.35 per hour, between October 2025 and March 2026, with new Blackwell capacity through August-September 2026 already booked on scarcity. Where H100 medians did fall — roughly halved to about $3.38 an hour by August 2026 — the analysis attributes the slide to specialist-cloud and marketplace competition and an aging chip, not to new external capacity. No dated pricing source attributes any AI-compute price move to SpaceX.

results.title: How much does an H100 cost per hour? | GPU Vista
highlights:
The H100 is the card most teams search for and the one most often misquoted. There is no single price: the same GPU rents for very different rates depending on where it sits and how the provider bills it.

Tracked rates · H100

100 in stock now

Floor

$0.79

From $0.53/hr (Vast.ai)

Median

$3.20

Ceiling

$10.38

38 providers tracked

India datacenter rate: from $3.51/hr (Jarvislabs)

## Why H100 prices vary so much

An H100 rate is a bundle, not a sticker. It includes the card, the host CPU and memory behind it, the network fabric between the cards, and the provider's power and cooling costs. Two providers can rent what looks like the same H100 and be selling quite different machines.

The spread widens further with the billing model. On-demand capacity is the most expensive because you can take it immediately. Spot or interruptible capacity is cheaper because the provider may reclaim it. Reserved contracts cost less per hour again, but you commit for weeks or months and pay whether you use the machine or not.

Above all of that sits supply. H100 capacity tightened through 2026 as training clusters absorbed the available stock, and neoclouds that bought early can undercut hyperscaler list prices significantly.

...

Most providers quote a per-GPU per-hour rate, but many sell whole nodes. An eight-GPU H100 node at a given per-GPU rate is eight times that rate per hour for the box, and you usually rent all eight whether your workload uses them or not.

That is why the tracked board always shows the whole-node rate beside the per-GPU rate whenever a node holds more than one card. Comparing a per-GPU number from one provider against a whole-node number from another is the single most common way to misread GPU pricing.

The other trap is billing granularity. Some providers charge per second, some per minute, some round to the hour. For a short job the rounding can matter more than the headline rate.

results.title: Nebius augmente de 21 % les prix de location des GPU face à l’envolée de la demande en infrastructures d’IA | Gate News
highlights:
- Nebius a annoncé une hausse de 21 % des prix de location des GPU à partir du 1er octobre 2024, après la hausse de 30 % de juin.
- Le prix de location à la demande du B300 de Nebius a augmenté de 56 % au total sur cinq mois.
- Oracle a renouvelé tous les contrats de GPU arrivés à expiration à des tarifs supérieurs de 20 % au cours de son trimestre précédent.

Le fournisseur de location de GPU Nebius a annoncé qu’il augmenterait jusqu’à 21 % les prix de location de GPU à la demande à partir du 1er octobre, selon un rapport publié le 22 septembre par Park Jae-hwan, analyste chez Eugene Investment & Securities. Cette hausse fait suite à une augmentation de 30 % des prix de l’ensemble des gammes de GPU le 1er juin, portant ainsi à environ 56 % en près de cinq mois la hausse du prix de location à la demande du B300 de Nebius. Eugene Investment attribue cette escalade continue des prix à la forte demande en infrastructures d’IA, dans un contexte d’intensification de la concurrence entre les développeurs de modèles d’IA. Oracle a également renouvelé au trimestre précédent tous ses contrats de GPU arrivés à expiration à des tarifs supérieurs de 20 %.

...

Nebius a décidé d’augmenter jusqu’à 21 % les prix de location de GPU à la demande à compter du 1er octobre, marquant la deuxième hausse depuis le 1er juin, date à laquelle l’entreprise avait augmenté de 30 % les prix de l’ensemble de sa gamme de GPU. Park Jae-hwan a indiqué que le prix de location à la demande du B300 de Nebius avait augmenté d’environ 56 % en près de cinq mois à la suite de ces ajustements successifs.

## Oracle renouvelle ses contrats de GPU avec une prime de 20 %

La tendance à la hausse des prix de location dépasse le cadre de Nebius. Oracle a révélé, lors de l’annonce de ses résultats du trimestre précédent, avoir renouvelé tous les contrats de GPU arrivés à expiration à des prix supérieurs de 20 % aux tarifs précédents. Park a déclaré que la prise en compte simultanée des hausses des prix de location sur les marchés spot et contractuels indiquait une accélération de la croissance des revenus des entreprises de néo-cloud et confirmait une nouvelle fois la vigueur de la demande en infrastructures d’IA.

results.title: AI Compute Futures: Nodal Exchange and the Race for GPU Trading
highlights:
- Nodal Exchange is expanding into AI computing capacity futures to leverage its dominance in power markets.
- CME Group plans to launch cash-settled GPU compute futures on October 5, 2026, focusing on Nvidia H100 and B200 indices.
- The shift treats AI compute as a commodity, similar to oil or electricity, to hedge against price volatility.
- Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) is also competing to establish a foothold in this nascent high-tech derivatives market.

...

The race to secure high-end chips has created a volatile environment for AI startups and established tech giants alike. When the availability of hardware fluctuates, the cost of renting compute power swings wildly. This instability has paved the way for financial instruments that allow companies to lock in prices for future capacity, effectively hedging against the risk of price spikes in the GPU rental market.

...

While Nodal leverages its energy roots, the CME Group is taking a direct approach to the hardware indices. The exchange has announced plans to launch cash-settled GPU compute futures on October 5, 2026. Unlike physical delivery contracts, these will be based on rental indices, specifically targeting the most coveted hardware in the industry: Nvidia’s H100 and B200 chips.

This specific focus on Nvidia hardware reflects the current market reality where a single vendor holds a near-monopoly on the high-end training chips required for Large Language Models. By creating a futures market for these specific chips, CME is providing a mechanism for enterprises to manage the cost of their AI roadmaps. If a company knows it will need massive clusters of B200s in late 2026, a futures contract allows them to fix their costs today, removing the uncertainty of spot-market pricing.

results.title: Nvidia H100 Prices Surge as AI Chip Supply Tightens
highlights:
Nvidia’s flagship H100 GPU now commands $25 000‑40 000 in 2026, while the B200 rental index jumped 24 % in March before retreating, underscoring a supply squeeze that is reshaping data‑center…

...

Nvidia’s flagship H100 GPU now commands $25 000‑40 000 in 2026, while the B200 rental index jumped 24 % in March before retreating, underscoring a supply squeeze that is reshaping data‑center economics. The price spike coincides with a broader memory crunch that threatens to curb AI‑driven growth across hyperscale clouds.

...

The H100 price band of $25 K‑40 K reflects both wafer scarcity and heightened demand from hyperscalers racing to expand AI clusters. Rental volatility, illustrated by the B200 index’s 24 % March surge, signals that cloud providers are passing on scarcity costs to end users. Anecdotal US‑East cloud rates now exceed $1 per hour for H100‑equipped instances, a level that pushes server‑price inflation above 15 % when memory premiums are added, according to recent customer disclosures.

## Memory Bottleneck Amplifies Chip Shortage

DRAM prices have exploded 700 % year‑over‑year as of July 2026, while high‑bandwidth memory (HBM) now consumes 23 % of DRAM wafer starts, up from 8 % in 2023. Demand for HBM4E outstrips supply by a factor of 1.4‑1.6, with SK Hynix holding 50‑55 % of the market and Samsung 40‑45 %; Micron’s volume production is delayed to 2027, extending a full‑scale ramp to 2028. Reddit threads report that hyperscalers have pre‑ordered almost all global DRAM for 2027, driving RAM prices up 500 % and leaving scant inventory for smartphones and PCs.

...

TSMC’s wafer output is already stretched by massive AI orders, limiting the advanced packaging slots that AMD can secure at the leading foundry. Early‑2026 data shows that 46 cents of every server‑CPU dollar now goes to chips from the challenger, overtaking the longtime leader in data‑center revenue for the first time. The Americas region, which houses roughly half of global data‑center capacity, is projected to grow supply at a 17 % compound annual rate, yet that expansion is throttled by the same packaging bottlenecks.
